title: Databases, abstraction and the ER model
subtitle: Why files were not enough, how a database hides storage details, and how to draw the world before building tables.

why.title: Why a DBMS
why.body: Storing data in separate files per application leads to redundancy, inconsistency (two copies disagree), no sharing or concurrent safety, and code tied to file formats. A DBMS keeps data in one place and provides a query language, integrity rules, concurrent access, security and recovery after failure. Applications: banking, airline reservation, universities, web sites.

abs.title: Three levels of abstraction
abs.body: The physical level describes how records are stored (files, indexes); the logical level describes what data exists and their relationships (tables); the view level shows each user only the part they need. Physical data independence: change the storage layout without changing the logical schema. Logical data independence: change the schema without rewriting every view or application. A schema is the design; an instance is the data at this moment.

er.title: The entity–relationship model
er.body: An entity is a distinguishable thing (Student, Course); an entity set is a collection of them. Attributes describe entities; a key attribute uniquely identifies one (studentID); composite, multivalued and derived attributes exist. A relationship associates entities (Student enrols in Course) with a cardinality: one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many. A weak entity has no key of its own and depends on an owner (Dependent of Employee).

gen.title: Specialisation, generalisation, aggregation
gen.body: Specialisation splits an entity set into subclasses (Employee → Teacher, Clerk) which inherit attributes; generalisation is the same idea seen bottom-up. Aggregation treats a relationship as an entity so it can take part in another relationship. Constraints: disjoint vs overlapping, total vs partial participation.

map.title: From ER to tables
map.body: Each strong entity becomes a table (key = primary key). A one-to-many relationship puts the “one” side’s key into the “many” table as a foreign key. A many-to-many relationship becomes its own table whose primary key is the pair of foreign keys, plus the relationship’s attributes. A weak entity’s table includes the owner’s key in its key.
map.steps: Student(id, name), Course(code, title) with a many-to-many “enrols with grade”. Tables: Student(id, name), Course(code, title), Enrolment(id → Student, code → Course, grade), primary key (id, code).

keys.title: Keys
keys.body: A superkey is any set of attributes that identifies a row; a candidate key is a minimal superkey; the primary key is the candidate chosen; a foreign key references another table’s key. Entity integrity: a primary key is never null. Referential integrity: a foreign key matches an existing key or is null.
